client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next week and I honestly don't feel ready at all. I've been working so many hours at my part-time job that I barely have time to study, and it feels like everything is just piling up on me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change the fact that I have way too much to do and not enough time.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the pressure of exams on top of long work hours is genuinely exhausting, and that feeling of things piling up makes complete sense. I also notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's a part of you that's questioning whether talking will even help, which tells me you might be feeling a bit hopeless or stuck right now. I'm curious — when you imagine getting through next week, what does that look like for you, even if it feels hard to picture?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to picture getting through next week, it just looks like... surviving, I guess. Like crawling to the finish line completely drained, not really feeling good about any of it. And yeah, you're right that part of me wonders what talking about it actually changes, because the exams and the shifts are still going to be there no matter what we say in here.
therapist: That image of just "surviving" and crawling to the finish line really captures how depleted you're already feeling, even before the week has started. You're right that talking won't make the exams or shifts disappear — but what it can do is help us figure out if the way you're thinking about this week is making it feel even heavier than it has to be. I'm wondering, when you say you won't feel good about any of it, what would "good enough" actually look like for you — is there any version of next week where you'd feel even a small sense of okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I try to picture a version of next week that feels "okay," I just draw a blank — like my brain won't even let me go there. I think part of me is scared to set any kind of bar, even a low one, because then I'll just feel worse when I don't clear it. It's like protecting myself from one more thing to fail at.
therapist: What you just described is such an important insight — that avoiding hope has become a way of protecting yourself, which makes a lot of sense given how overwhelmed you are right now. I notice there's a real urgency in how you're expressing this, like this fear of failing runs pretty deep and feels very present for you in this moment. I'm curious — when you think about "failing," what does that actually mean to you, and whose voice does that word come in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I hadn't really thought about whose voice it is. But honestly, when I hear the word "failing," it's... it's my own voice, but it sounds a lot like my dad's — like this disappointed, quiet kind of judgment that doesn't even need to say much to cut deep. And failing, to me, means proving that I was never really capable in the first place, like all the doubt people had about me was justified all along.
therapist: That took real courage to name, and what you've just uncovered is significant — that the voice judging you has roots that go way back, long before these exams. The idea that struggling would *prove* you were never capable is such a painful belief to carry, and I imagine it makes every challenge feel like it's on trial for something much bigger than just one test. I want to gently ask — is there any evidence in your life, even small moments, that contradicts that story of never really being capable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I guess there have been moments. Like, I did get through that really brutal statistics course last semester, even when I was convinced I was going to fail. But it's hard to hold onto that right now, because my brain just immediately goes "yeah, but that was different, you got lucky, this time it's real."
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence that contradicts the "never capable" story, and your brain immediately moved to dismiss it with "that was luck, this time is different." That pattern of discounting your own wins is actually a very common thinking trap, and it's worth noticing how quickly and automatically it kicked in just now. I'm curious — if a close friend had gotten through that brutal statistics course the same way you did, would you tell them it was just luck?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, no, I wouldn't tell a friend that. I'd probably say they worked hard and figured it out, even if it was messy. But it still feels different when it's me — like I can see the logic of what you're saying, but it doesn't actually land emotionally, you know?
therapist: That gap between "I get it logically but it doesn't *feel* true" is one of the most honest and common experiences in this kind of work — and it actually makes sense, because that belief about not being capable has had years to take root emotionally, so it won't shift just from one good argument. I also notice there's something in how you're saying this that feels a little urgent or stirred up, like this is touching something that matters a lot to you right now. What do you think it would take — not to be convinced by logic, but to actually *feel* like that statistics course victory was really yours?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what would actually make it feel real is if someone I respected — like a professor or a peer — genuinely acknowledged it, not just a grade on a paper. But that's the thing, even when people do say something positive, I kind of brush it off or assume they're just being nice. It's like there's this filter that blocks anything good from actually landing.
therapist: You've just described the filter so clearly — external validation can't get in because there's already a verdict in place that decides it isn't trustworthy, which means the only voice that ever really gets through is the critical one. That's an exhausting and lonely way to live, and I notice as you're describing it, there's an energy in your voice that sounds almost frustrated or resigned, like part of you is tired of this pattern even as you're naming it. I'm wondering — when you imagine life without that filter, even just for a moment, what feels scary about actually letting the good stuff land?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I'm definitely tired of it, you're right about that. But when I try to imagine actually letting the good stuff in... I think what scares me is that if I believe it, and then it turns out to be wrong or it goes away, that's going to hurt so much more than if I just never let it in at all. It's like I've built this wall to protect myself from a bigger disappointment, and tearing it down feels genuinely dangerous.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really profound and protective logic — if you never fully believe in yourself, you can't be devastated when things fall apart, and that wall has probably kept you safe in some real ways. But I'm also hearing something underneath that, almost like grief — like part of you is mourning all the good things that wall has also kept out. I want to sit with this question with you: is it possible that the disappointment you're so afraid of is actually something you've *already been living with*, just in a quieter, more constant form?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

therapist: That moment of not being able to push back — that's not defeat, that's actually a really rare kind of honesty with yourself, and it takes a lot to sit with something that true.
